title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
authors: Edgar Josué Landinez Borda, Ravindra Shinde, Claudia Filippi, Markus Holzmann, Saverio Moroni
abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.
summary: This work uses Quantum Monte Carlo methods to study excitons in solid molecular hydrogen under compression, comparing results against BSE and TDDFT. The key finding is that while excitation energies may agree, the description of exciton localization and response properties varies significantly between theoretical approaches. This highlights the critical importance of the chosen many-body formalism when analyzing correlated electronic excitations.
main_problem: The study investigates the nature and spatial extent of the lowest neutral excitation (exciton) in solid molecular hydrogen under varying levels of compression.
main_result: The authors find that while QMC excitation energies show good agreement across methods, the exciton localization and associated responses (like transition dipole moments) differ significantly between QMC, BSE, and TDDFT, especially in the insulating regime.
method: The research employs advanced electronic structure methods, primarily Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, and compares results against the Bethe-Salpeter Equation (BSE) and Time-Dependent DFT (TDDFT).
model_or_system: The physical system is solid molecular hydrogen (H2) in phase-I, studied as a function of increasing external compression, which changes the electronic correlation regime.
key_observables: Exciton binding energy, exciton localization (analyzed via $\Delta S(\mathbf{k})$ and $\Deltaho(\mathbf{r})$), transition dipole moment ($\mu_{01}$), and excitation-induced forces ($\Delta F_A$).
important_parameters: Compression/density ($ho/ho_0$), which drives the system from an insulating to a semiconducting regime.
main_assumptions: The Born-Oppenheimer approximation is used, and the comparison highlights the systematic differences arising from the choice of excited-state wave function expansion (e.g., single-CSF vs. multideterminant CIS).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the neutral excitation gap vs. density for multiple methods, the coefficient $c_{2	ext{max}}$ showing the transition from multi-pair to single-pair dominance, and the small-$k$ behavior of the static structure factor difference $\Delta S(\mathbf{k})$.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares results from QMC, BSE, and TDDFT across various observables (energy, localization, forces) as a function of density, emphasizing that localization properties are highly sensitive to the theoretical framework used.
why_interesting: The detailed comparison of multiple correlated electronic structure methods (QMC, BSE, TDDFT) to characterize excitonic properties in a simple molecular solid provides crucial insights into the limitations and strengths of modern many-body theories for correlated materials.
